title: The Fosbury Flop and the Science of High Jumping
summary: In 1968, Dick Fosbury crossed the bar backwards and changed athletics forever. The high jump is a sport of physics, nerve, and extraordinary technique. Here's how the best in the world do it.
content:
In the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, an American athlete named Dick Fosbury crossed the high jump bar in a way nobody had seen before. Where previous jumpers had gone over face-down — the straddle technique, or the Western Roll before it — Fosbury went over face-up, arching his back so that his body cleared the bar in sections. His head went first, then his shoulders and back, then his hips, then his legs. Each part of his body was above the bar only briefly, and his centre of gravity — the mathematical point at which his body's mass was centred — passed below the bar throughout the jump.

Fosbury won the gold medal. Within a decade, every elite high jumper in the world was using his technique. The Fosbury Flop had not just improved on existing approaches — it had revealed that clearing a high jump bar and lifting your centre of gravity over that bar were two different problems, and that the second problem was significantly easier than the first.

The Physics of the Flop

The insight the Fosbury Flop exploited is that a jumper's centre of gravity does not need to clear the bar — only each part of the body does, and not simultaneously. By arching the back over the bar, the jumper creates a curved body shape in which the centre of gravity is actually below the bar throughout the jump. The body clears the bar in sequence — head, then back, then hips, then legs — but the mass is never entirely above the bar at once.

This is physically efficient in a way that face-down techniques cannot match. Face-down, the entire body must rise above the bar simultaneously, which requires lifting the centre of gravity well above the bar's height. Face-up, with the arch, the centre of gravity stays lower. The energy required is proportionally less. The technique allows jumpers to clear heights their physiology would not otherwise permit.

The Approach Run

What is least understood by those who watch high jumping is the importance of the approach run. The jump itself — the moment of takeoff and the arc over the bar — is built on the kinetic energy and body position generated in the last few strides of the approach. The approach is not a straight line but a curve, bringing the jumper to the bar at an angle that sets up the rotation and arch of the Flop.

The final stride before takeoff is the most critical. The jumper must plant the takeoff foot at exactly the right position and angle, with exactly the right speed, while simultaneously beginning the backward lean that will produce the arch over the bar. Too early a lean and the energy is wasted. Too late and there is no time to arch before the bar. The timing, repeated thousands of times in training, must become automatic.

The jump is over in less than a second. The approach run is where everything that makes the jump possible is built. When I plant my foot for the last time, everything after that is already determined. The arc, the arch, the clearance — they were decided in the approach. The jump is just the consequence.

Mutaz Essa Barshim and the Modern Standard

Qatar's Mutaz Essa Barshim, alongside Sweden's Armand Duplantis in pole vault, has been the face of field event excellence in the modern era. Barshim's personal best of 2.43 metres — set in 2014 and equalling the world record — reflects the combination of exceptional physical attributes and refined technique that elite high jumping demands. His long limbs give him natural leverage. His approach speed is high for his height. His arch over the bar is controlled and precise.

The image most associated with Barshim is from the Tokyo Olympics — his decision, alongside Italy's Gianmarco Tamberi, to share the gold medal when both athletes had cleared 2.37 metres and both failed at 2.39 metres. It was a moment that captured something essential about athletics: competition at its limit, two athletes who had given everything, and a choice to celebrate together rather than continue the battle that neither could win.

What Limits the High Jump

The high jump world record has not improved significantly in decades, which raises the question of what the human limit is. The answer involves both physical constraints — the ratio of power to weight that determines how high a human body can be propelled — and the limits of technique. The Fosbury Flop extracted most of the efficiency gains available from the physics of the event. Further improvements require athletes who are faster, stronger, and taller, with better-trained takeoffs and more precise arches. The improvements have come slowly, because those requirements are genuinely rare in combination.
